mcqs.question: What does the `lowbit` operation, `i & (-i)`, compute, and why is it central to a Fenwick tree's algorithm?
options: It computes the number of set bits in i, used to determine tree height
It isolates the lowest set bit of i, and adding or subtracting it moves between the implicit ranges each array slot is responsible for — the entire mechanism behind update and query
It computes i divided by 2, used to walk toward the root like a binary heap
It converts i from 0-indexed to 1-indexed
mcqs.explanation: In two's complement, `i & (-i)` isolates exactly the lowest set bit of i, and that value tells you the size of the range slot i is responsible for — adding it during update or subtracting it during query is precisely how the algorithm navigates the tree's implicit structure without explicit pointers. It doesn't count set bits, it isn't a heap-style halving operation, and it isn't an indexing-conversion utility on its own.

mcqs.question: Why do Fenwick trees conventionally use 1-indexing internally, even for problems with naturally 0-indexed arrays?
options: 1-indexing is required by convention only, with no technical reason
0-indexing would use more memory than 1-indexing
The lowbit trick breaks at index 0, since `0 & (-0)` is 0 and would prevent the update/query loops from moving correctly
Fenwick trees cannot represent arrays of even length using 0-indexing
mcqs.explanation: Index 0 is a genuine special case for the lowbit operation — it produces 0, which breaks the loop that's supposed to advance through slot indices — so the structure is built 1-indexed and callers apply a consistent offset when their own array is 0-indexed. This isn't a memory concern or an arbitrary convention with no technical basis, and it has nothing to do with array length parity.

mcqs.question: Why does `range_sum(l, r) = prefix_sum(r) - prefix_sum(l-1)` work for sum but not for an equivalent formula using min?
options: Subtraction exactly inverts addition, so removing everything before l from a sum is well-defined; there's no equivalent way to 'un-min' a value, since min has no inverse operation
The formula actually does work identically for min, just with different function names
This formula only works when l equals 1
Min queries require the array to be sorted first, unlike sum queries
mcqs.explanation: Sum's invertibility is what makes the subtraction trick valid — subtracting exactly cancels out the contribution of everything before l. Min has no operation that reverses its effect, so there's no way to compute 'min excluding everything before l' from two prefix-min values alone. The formula genuinely fails for min (not merely under a different name), it holds for any valid l ≥ 1, and neither version requires a sorted array.

mcqs.question: Why does supporting range update AND range query (sum) simultaneously require two Fenwick trees instead of the single-tree difference-array trick?
options: The single-tree difference-array trick only supports point queries (recovering one value), not summing over an arbitrary range, so an additional structure is needed to make range queries work too
Two trees are needed because Fenwick trees can only store even numbers of elements
This is a common misconception — a single difference-array tree actually does support range queries directly
The second tree exists purely for redundancy in case of data corruption
mcqs.explanation: The difference-array trick alone reconstructs a single value via a prefix sum, but summing a whole range with that same single tree doesn't produce the correct total — a second tree carries additional bookkeeping that the algebraic derivation requires to make range sums come out correctly. This isn't about even element counts or redundancy for corruption — it's a genuine mathematical requirement for the range-sum formula to hold.

mcqs.question: A problem needs range-maximum queries with frequent point updates. Why would a Fenwick tree be a poor fit compared to a segment tree here?
options: Fenwick trees are always slower than segment trees regardless of operation
Max isn't invertible the way sum is, so the subtraction-based prefix-query trick a Fenwick tree relies on doesn't have a natural equivalent for max
Fenwick trees cannot support point updates at all
Segment trees require less code than Fenwick trees for any operation
mcqs.explanation: Fenwick trees lean on invertibility (subtraction undoes addition) to compose range answers from prefix answers; max has no such inverse, so there's no natural way to adapt the Fenwick approach to it, while a segment tree handles max directly with no such requirement. Fenwick trees are actually faster with a lower constant factor for operations they do support, they support point updates natively (that's their core operation), and segment trees generally require more code, not less, for standard sum-like operations.
